questions.question: 34608. Fluoride is least effective in which area
questions.explain:
Pits and fissures are enamel faults that harbour food and microorganisms are the most important anatomical features
leading to the development of occlusal caries. Even though fluorides are highly effective in reducing the smooth surface caries, unfortunately they are not effective in protecting the occlusal pits and fissures where 90% of all carious lesions
occur.

questions.question: 34607. In acute fluoride toxicity we use:

questions.question:
34603. Identify the disadvantage of cohort 
studies:
questions.option2: Several outcomes related to exposure is studied simultaneously
questions.option3: A direct estimate of relative risk is provided
questions.option4: Takes a long time to complete the study
questions.explain:
Advantages

Incidence can be directly calculated
Direct estimation of the relative risk (RR)
More than one outcome of the risk factor can be studied.
 Dose response relationship with exposure can be studied
Temporal association of the exposure with the outcome can be seen
Certain biases like recall bias, interviewer’s bias are not a problem.
Disadvantages

The major disadvantage is the huge requirement for resources, viz. time, money and personnel
Unsuitable for rare diseases
Long periods of follow up needed
Attrition is a problem as long follow up is required
Ethical problems are more because as evidence of the RF accumulates, it becomes the duty of the investigator to educate those with the risk factor. Wait and watch may be unethical
Only one or a few risk factors can be studied.

questions.question: 34602. 48. A single force applied at which point of a tooth will allow complete translation of the tooth:
questions.explain:
Tipping is simple type of tooth movement where a single force is applied to the crown, which results in movement of the crown in the direction of the force and the root in
opposite direction.
• Pure translation is brought about when the line of action of an applied force passes through the centre of resistance of a tooth.

questions.question: 34601. Prolonged retention of primary tooth may lead to
questions.option1: Altered path of permanent tooth eruption
questions.option4: Warping of roots of adjacent teeth
questions.explain:
over-retained or persistent primary teeth, occurs when a baby tooth remains in the mouth beyond its expected exfoliation (shedding) time. This can happen due to various factors, most commonly the absence of a permanent tooth to push the primary tooth out. While sometimes harmless, prolonged retention can lead to complications like malocclusion (misalignment of teeth) and require dental treatment.  
Causes:
Absence of Permanent Tooth:
The most frequent reason is the lack of a permanent tooth to erupt and resorb the root of the primary tooth.  
Genetic Predisposition:
Some individuals may have a genetic tendency towards missing permanent teeth.  
Developmental Issues:
Problems with the development of permanent teeth can also lead to prolonged retention.  
Dental Caries and Infections:
Tooth decay and infections can affect root resorption.  
Ankylosis:
In rare cases, the primary tooth can fuse to the jawbone, preventing its natural exfoliation.  
Complications:
Malocclusion:
Over-retained teeth can shift the position of adjacent teeth, causing crowding or misalignment.  
Space Closure:
The space left by the retained tooth might close, potentially blocking the eruption of other permanent teeth.  
Root Resorption of Adjacent Teeth:
The retained tooth can exert pressure on neighboring teeth, causing their roots to be resorbed.  
Difficulty Eating and Speaking:
In some cases, the retained tooth can interfere with normal chewing and speech.

questions.question: 34600. In a true combined lesion, which treatment is performed first?
questions.explain: Endo is done first to eliminate infection; perio therapy follows based on healing response.

34599. Which of the following is NOT a transient/ self correcting

questions.question: 34598. Most of leeway space is contributed by
questions.explain:
Most of the leeway space is contributed by primary second molar due to significant difference in size between it and
second premolar

questions.question: 34597. Difference in width of permanent and primary incisors is
questions.explain:
The permanent incisors are usually larger than the deciduous. This difference between amount of space needed for the accommodation of the incisors and
the amount of space available is called incisal liability. The incisal liability is about 7mm in maxillary arch and about 5mm in mandibular arch.
The incisal liability is overcome by:
• Utilizing physiologic spaces in primary dentition.
• Increase in inter canine width
• More labial inclination of permanent incisors.

questions.question: 34596. Ugly duckling stage affects
questions.explain: Ugly duckling stage is seen in maxillary central incisor region between 8 -9 years of age. This condition is seen during eruption of permanent canines

questions.question: 34595. Which of the following is an early clinical sign of dehydration?
questions.explain: One of the earliest signs of dehydration is dryness of the mouth and mucous membranes.

questions.question: 34594. Which factor most significantly influences the apical seal during obturation?
questions.explain: Precise working length ensures obturation material reaches the correct apical extent without over- or underfilling, directly impacting the seal.

questions.question: 34593. Strip perforation is most commonly seen in:
questions.explain:
Strip Perforation
A lateral perforation of the root canal wall, usually due to excessive instrumentation or thinning of dentin in curved or narrow roots.

Common Site:
- Mesial root of mandibular molars (danger zone on furcal side)

Causes:
- Over-preparation of the canal
- Use of large files in curved canals
- Inadequate knowledge of root anatomy

Signs:
- Sudden bleeding
- Sudden loss of resistance during instrumentation
- Radiographic signs (lateral radiolucency or file seen outside canal)

questions.question: 34592. The ideal length of obturation in a completed root canal treatment is:
questions.explain:
Obturation Length in Endodontics:

- Ideal Length:
0.5 to 1 mm short of the radiographic apex
(corresponds to the apical constriction, the narrowest part of the canal)

questions.question: 34591. What is the main function of EDTA in endodontics?
questions.explain:
Function of EDTA in Endodontics

- Smear layer removal: Chelates calcium ions from dentin to remove the inorganic component of the smear layer
- Opens dentinal tubules: Enhances penetration of irrigants and sealers
- Lubrication: Reduces friction during instrumentation
- Improves disinfection: Allows better access for irrigants to act effectively

Usually used after sodium hypochlorite as a final rinse.

questions.question: 34590. Glass ionomer cement chemically bonds to tooth structure through:
questions.option3: Ionic bond with calcium in dentin
questions.explain:
Bonding of Glass Ionomer Cement (GIC)

Type of Bond:
- Chemical bond to tooth structure
- Ionic interaction between carboxyl groups in polyacrylic acid (in GIC) and calcium ions in enamel and dentin

Steps for Bonding:
1. Cavity cleaning – Remove debris without desiccating dentin
2. Conditioning – Apply 10–20% polyacrylic acid for 10 seconds to remove smear layer and improve bonding
3. Rinse and blot dry – Keep surface moist (do not overdry)
4. Place GIC – It chemically bonds to moist tooth surface without need for bonding agent

questions.question: 34589. The ideal depth for a Class I amalgam cavity preparation is:
questions.explain:
Class I Cavity Preparation for Amalgam

Indication
For carious lesions on:
- Occlusal surfaces of molars and premolars
- Occlusal 2/3 of buccal or lingual surfaces
- Pits of maxillary incisors

Outline Form
- Follows the pits and fissures
- Smooth, flowing walls without sharp corners
- Conservative but includes all carious areas

Resistance Form
- Flat pulpal floor (1.5–2 mm deep)
- Box-shaped cavity with strong marginal ridges
- Avoid weak enamel walls

Retention Form
- Slight convergence of buccal and lingual walls
- No undercuts needed due to amalgam’s compressive strength

Convenience Form
- Adequate access for instrumentation and material placement

Cavosurface Margin
- 90° angle to prevent fracture of amalgam
- No beveling required

Final Steps
- Remove any remaining caries
- Clean and dry cavity before placing amalgam

questions.question: 34588. In the sandwich technique used in restorative dentistry, which material is typically placed first against the dentin?
questions.explain:
In the sandwich technique, glass ionomer cement (GIC) is placed first against dentin.
- It bonds chemically to dentin and releases fluoride.
- Then composite resin is layered over GIC for better esthetics and strength.

questions.question: 34587. A 30-year-old patient presents with a necrotic pulp in a mandibular molar. The canal shows a sharp curvature in the apical third. What is the most appropriate instrumentation technique?
questions.explain:
Canal Preparation in Curved Canals

Challenges
- High risk of ledge formation, transportation, and instrument separation
- Uneven dentin removal if not properly managed

Key Steps
- Establish glide path with small hand files (size 08 to 15)
- Use flexible NiTi instruments for better adaptation to curvature
- Apply gentle pressure; avoid forcing the file
- Prefer crown-down or step-back technique for controlled shaping
- Use lubricants like EDTA gel to reduce friction
- Irrigate frequently with sodium hypochlorite to flush out debris
- Check working length and canal patency regularly
- Avoid over-enlargement of curved areas to prevent weakening

questions.question: 34586. Which of the following is a major drawback of calcium hydroxide?
questions.explain:
Enterococcus faecalis in Root Canal

Enterococcus faecalis is a gram-positive, facultative anaerobic bacterium commonly found in failed root canal treatments.

Key Features
- Resistant to high pH, including calcium hydroxide
- Survives in nutrient-poor, harsh environments
- Forms biofilm and invades dentinal tubules
- Tolerates heat and disinfectants better than many oral bacteria

Role in Endodontics
- Frequently isolated in persistent periapical infections
- Associated with post-treatment apical periodontitis
- Hard to eliminate with standard irrigants and intracanal medicaments

Management
- Use of advanced irrigants like sodium hypochlorite and chlorhexidine
- Activation of irrigants (e.g., ultrasonic or sonic)
- Use of bioceramic sealers with antibacterial properties
- Emphasis on complete cleaning, shaping, and coronal seal to prevent reinfection

questions.question: 34585. In the paper point method, working length is confirmed by:
questions.option2: Length at which paper point exits the apex
questions.option3: Appearance of blood or moisture at the tip
questions.explain:
Paper Point Working Length

Purpose
- Confirms working length in cases where radiographs or apex locators are unreliable
- Helps detect apical bleeding or exudate, indicating inflammation or perforation
- Ensures the canal is dried up to the correct length before obturation

Procedure
- Insert paper point into canal to the estimated working length
- Remove and observe for moisture or blood
- Adjust length if the paper point is overextended or too short

Note
Used mainly in teeth with open apex, exudative canals, or after apex locator confirmation.

questions.question: 34584. Bioceramic sealers are preferred in modern endodontics due to:
questions.option3: Bioactivity and chemical bonding to dentin
questions.explain:
Bioceramic,ceramic based sealers are bioactive, form hydroxyapatite, and bond chemically to dentin.

Composition
Common components include calcium silicates, calcium phosphates, calcium hydroxide, and zirconium oxide.

Types and Uses
- MTA (Mineral Trioxide Aggregate): pulp capping, apexification, perforation repair
- Biodentine: dentin substitute, pulp therapy
- EndoSequence BC Sealer: root canal sealer
- BioAggregate: similar to MTA with better handling

Properties
- Excellent biocompatibility
- Promotes hard tissue formation
- Sets in moisture
- Antibacterial due to high pH
- Dimensionally stable

questions.question: 34583. First sign of tetanus is:
questions.explain:
Trismus (lockjaw) is the earliest and most common sign of tetanus caused by the neurotoxin tetanospasmin.
Later signs include muscle rigidity, spasms and opisthotonus. Neck stiffness and fever are nonspecific.
(Ref: Cawson+ Macleod Clinical medicine)

questions.question: 34582. Which of the following is a key sign in anaphylactic shock?
questions.explain:
Anaphylactic shock is a severe, lifethreatening allergic reaction involving IgE mediated hypersensitivity.  It leads to widespread vasodilation (causing hypotension) and increased capillary permeability. Urticaria (hives) is a hallmark skin manifestation, often with angioedema. Bradycardia is uncommon; tachycardia usually occurs.  Cyanosis and clubbing are chronic findings and hemoptysis suggests lung pathology, not anaphylaxis.
Hence, urticaria with hypotension is a classic sign.
(Ref: Cawson+ Davidson)

questions.question: 34581. A 65year old hypertensive diabetic presents with shortness of breath and orthopnea.  Bilateral basal crepitations are heard.  What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explain:
The classic symptoms of Congestive Heart Failure (CHF) include dyspnea, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.  Basal crepitations are due to pulmonary congestion from leftsided heart failure. Risk factors like age, hypertension and diabetes increase the likelihood of cardiac dysfunction.
COPD may also cause breathlessness, but crepitations are not typical.  Pneumonia causes localized findings and fever and pulmonary embolism typically presents with acute chest pain and tachypnea, not orthopnea.Thus, CHF is the most likely diagnosis in this clinical scenario.
(Ref: Davidson)

questions.question: 34580. Commonest cause of postoperative fever on day 1 is:
questions.explain:
Atelectasis (collapse of alveoli) is the most common cause of fever within 24 hours postoperatively, especially after abdominal/thoracic surgery. Wound infections and DVT occur later (days 3–5), and UTI may take longer to develop.
(Ref:Bailey and love's + Makkhan lal)

questions.question: 34579. What is the main cause of wound dehiscence?
questions.explain:
Wound dehiscence refers to partial or complete separation of a surgical incision. Infection weakens the tissue and suture strength, increasing the risk.
Other factors include malnutrition, obesity or poor surgical technique, but infection remains the most common cause.
(Ref: Bailey and Love's)

questions.question: 34578. Which of the following is most commonly associated with sinus tract formation?
questions.explain: Sinus tract is typical of chronic periapical abscess as a drainage mechanism.

questions.question: 34577. According to ergonomic best practices in operative dentistry, which operator position is preferred for right-handed practitioners?
questions.explain:
Operator’s Position in Dentistry

Maintains efficiency, visibility, and reduces physical strain.

General Guidelines
- Back straight, shoulders relaxed
- Thighs parallel to the floor
- Feet flat on the floor or footrest
- Elbows close to the body at right angles
- Forearms parallel to the floor
- Minimal head tilt forward

Clock Positions for Right-Handed Operator
- 7 o’clock: Anterior surfaces facing the operator
- 9 o’clock: Buccal surfaces of lower posterior teeth
- 11 o’clock: Most common and ergonomic, allows access to most areas
- 12 o’clock: Lingual surfaces of lower anterior teeth

Left-handed operators use opposite clock positions (1 to 5 o’clock)

questions.question: 34576. Keratin pearls in biopsy are pathognomonic for:
questions.explain:
Squamous Cell Carcinoma 
Histopathology Features:

Invasive nests or sheets of malignant squamous cells
Keratin pearl formation
Cellular atypia and pleomorphism
Increased mitotic figures
Possible invasion into underlying connective tissue

questions.question: 34575. Salivary tumor with mucous and epidermoid cells is:
questions.explain:
Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma 

Common Sites
Parotid gland (most common)
Minor salivary glands, especially palate

Clinical Features
Slow-growing painless swelling
May cause pain or facial nerve weakness in advanced cases
Can occur at any age

Histology
Mixture of mucous-producing cells and squamous cells
Graded as low, intermediate, or high grade based on cellular atypia and growth pattern

Radiographic Features
May cause bone destruction if arising in minor glands of the jaws

Treatment
Surgical excision with clear margins
Radiotherapy for high-grade or unresectable tumors

questions.question: 34574. A patient with hemorrhagic shock will most likely show:
questions.explain:
Haemorrhagic Shock
Clinical Features:

Pale, cold, clammy skin
Rapid, weak pulse
Low blood pressure

Decreased urine output

questions.question: 34572. One hallmark of cancer is sustaining proliferative signaling. Which mechanism most directly achieves this?
questions.explain:
One hallmark of cancer is the ability to sustain proliferative signaling, meaning cancer cells can continuously grow and divide without normal regulatory controls. This is most directly achieved by mutations that activate oncogenes such as Ras, which promote cell growth and division.

- Increased p53 activity (ক) would suppress proliferation by causing cell cycle arrest or apoptosis, so it is not correct.
- Activation of tumor suppressor genes (গ) also inhibits cell growth, acting against cancer progression.
- Inhibition of telomerase (ঘ) limits cellular lifespan; cancer cells often activate telomerase to maintain immortality.

Thus, mutations activating oncogenes like Ras allow cells to bypass normal growth controls and proliferate continuously.

questions.question: 34571. Which theory explains dentin hypersensitivity due to fluid movement in tubules stimulating nerves?
questions.explain:
Theories of dentin hypersensitivity

1. Hydrodynamic theory
Pain results from fluid movement within dentinal tubules that stimulates nerve endings

2. Neural theory
Direct stimulation of nerve fibers in the dentin causes pain

3. Odontoblast receptor theory
Odontoblasts function as receptors sending signals to adjacent nerves

questions.question: 34570. Which characteristic of paraformaldehyde-based mummifying agents led to their disuse in modern endodontics?
questions.option1: Tissue toxicity and potential systemic effects
questions.explain:
Disadvantages of Paraformaldehyde

- Highly toxic and irritant to skin, eyes, and respiratory tract
- Carcinogenic potential with prolonged exposure
- Strong pungent odor
- Causes tissue fixation artifacts if not used properly
- Limited penetration in some tissues
- Requires careful handling and storage

questions.question: 34569. What sets aspirin’s action apart from other NSAIDs?
questions.option4: Has no effect on platelet aggregation
questions.explain: Aspirin acetylates COX irreversibly, extending its antiplatelet action beyond its plasma half-life.

questions.question: 34568. Which is not false?
questions.option3: Fusion- Separated crown from one tooth germ
questions.option4: Gemination - Union of two teeth from two tooth germ
questions.explain:
Dilaceration - Angulation of root /extraordinary curvature in the roots resulting from trauma during root development.  Such type of tooth is called hook shaped tooth.

Concrescence - Fusion of the root in the socket by cementum. In this conditions, PDL is absent in the root. 

Gemination /Twinning : separated crown with single root canal from single tooth germ is called gemination. Commonly seen in maxillary  incisor region 

Fusion : Union or fusion of two teeth from two tooth germ. 

ref: Cawson,Nisha Garg

questions.question: 34567. True about human dentition except:

questions.option4: Shovel shaped incisors common in negro
questions.explain:
Human dentition :

1.Shovel shaped incisors common in mongoloid people. Uncommon in negro. Incisal edge shows mamelons 

2.Canines with longest,strongest root are last tooth to be lost,least affected by caries,four corner stones of dental arches & Guide-posts in occlusion  

3. Permanent  premolars are miniature of a molar but may regarded as canine functionally.

4.Upper deciduous 2nd molar is a replica of 1st permanent molar hence similarity is called
isomorphy.

ref: A K DAS, Scott & Symons

questions.question: 34566. Tubercle's of Carabelli:
questions.explain:
Casp of Carabelli / Tubercle of Carabelli:

Described by George C Carabelli:
- Lingual aspect of the mesio-lingual cusp is called fifth cusp/a pit/a groove/ casp of Carabelli. 
- Found in deciduous second molar and permanent 1st molars.
- More frequent in White races
- Low prevalence of tubercles of Carabelli in Mongoloid dentition.

Ref: A K DAS, Scott & Symons

questions.question: 34565. Which brain region primarily regulates respiratory rhythm?
questions.explain:
Here’s a quick overview of the brain regions and what they mainly control:

- Cerebellum
Coordinates voluntary movements, balance, and posture

- Medulla oblongata
Controls vital autonomic functions like breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure

- Hypothalamus
Regulates homeostasis, temperature, hunger, thirst, and hormonal control via the pituitary

- Pons
Assists in regulating breathing patterns and relays signals between cerebrum and cerebellum

questions.question: 34564. In the loop of Henle, the thick ascending limb is:
questions.option1: Permeable to water, impermeable to NaCl
questions.option2: Impermeable to water, actively transports NaCl
questions.explain: The thick ascending limb is impermeable to water and actively reabsorbs NaCl—essential for urine concentration.

questions.question: 34563. Which zone of the adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone?
questions.explain:
The adrenal cortex is divided into:

Glomerulosa → Mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)
Fasciculata → Glucocorticoids (cortisol)
Reticularis → Androgens
